slides.title: 1.1 Sport and Economy
content: Introduction to the relationship between sport and the economy.
Economy defined: production, distribution, trade, and consumption of goods and services.
Sport is a major economic sector creating jobs and business opportunities.
Links with education, real estate, and tourism.

slides.title: Economic Impact of Athletes
content: Ethiopian athletes like Haile Gebresilassie, Derartu Tulu, and Kenenisa Bekele have invested in hotels, agriculture, manufacturing, and other sectors.
International examples: Cristiano Ronaldo (CR7 Hotels, Fitness), Samuel Eto'o (Betting Platform), Didier Drogba (Bank, Foundation).
These investments create jobs and contribute to economic growth.

slides.title: Impact of Sporting Events
content: Hosting international events like the CECAFA Cup generates significant economic activity.
Spending on hotel rooms, car rentals, food, flights, uniforms, equipment, and advertising.
This stimulates the local economy and benefits various service providers.

slides.title: 1.2 Sport and Gender
content: Gender refers to the social construction of men and women, influencing behaviors and expectations in sport.
Women's participation in sport has been limited historically by division and separation.
Benefits of sport include stress management, communication skills, and the ability to work well with others.

slides.title: Milestones for Women in Sport
content: Helene Madison (USA): First woman to swim 100-yard freestyle in one minute (1932 Olympics).
Nawal El Moutawakel (Morocco): First woman from an Arab country to win an Olympic medal (1984).
Kathrine Switzer: First woman to run the Boston Marathon despite opposition (1967).
Tigist Gezahagn (Ethiopia): First Ethiopian gold medalist at the Paralympics (T13 1500m).

slides.title: Women in Ethiopian Sport
content: Derartu Tulu: First Ethiopian woman to win 10,000m and later President of the Ethiopian Athletic Federation.
Fatuma Roba: First Ethiopian woman to win a marathon.
Lidiya Tafesse: First Ethiopian female international football referee.
Loza Abera: First professional Ethiopian female footballer.

slides.title: Human Rights and Gender Equality
content: UNESCO states that access to physical education and sport is a fundamental right for all.
The Ethiopian Constitution (Article 35) guarantees equal rights for women.
Sport is a tool for social empowerment, reinforcing women's and girls' capabilities.
Goal: Achieving gender equality in sport participation and treatment.

slides.title: 1.3 Sport and Technology
content: Technology has been integral to sports for a long time, especially in elite competitions.
Wearable technology: Fitness trackers, smart clothing (T-shirts, socks, sensor-enabled shoes).
These track speed, force, movement, and traction for performance analysis.
eSports: Competitive gaming, a fast-growing sector built around digital technology.

slides.title: Technology in Officiating
content: Goal-line technology: Determines if the ball has wholly passed the goal line.
Video Assistant Referee (VAR): Used in football to review goals, penalty decisions, direct red card incidents, and mistaken identity.
VAR assists the referee in making accurate decisions, reducing errors.
Technology ensures fair play and improves the quality of the game.

slides.title: Technology in Athletics
content: Stopwatches and photo-finish cameras used for accurate timing and measurement.
Performance tracking systems help analyze and improve athlete performance.
Advanced equipment and facility design enhance training and competition.

slides.title: 1.4 Consequence of Doping
content: Doping: The use of prohibited substances or methods to enhance performance.
Considered cheating, destroying the spirit of fair competition.
Health risks: Unsterile injections can lead to HIV/AIDS, hepatitis, and other diseases.
Athletes are urged to say no to doping and compete clean.

slides.title: Consequences of Doping
content: Health Consequences: Risks of infection, organ damage, mental health issues.
Sport Consequences (Sanctions): Disqualification, loss of medals, bans from sport (up to 4 years or life).
Financial penalties and publication of violations.
Social Consequences: Damage to reputation, public humiliation, media scrutiny.
Doping rule violations affect the athlete's family and friends.

slides.title: 2.1 Body System and Exercise
content: The human body has 11 organ systems, including cardiovascular, respiratory, and muscular.
Short-term effects of exercise: Increased heart rate, faster breathing, more blood flow to muscles.
Long-term effects: Improved heart and lung efficiency, stronger muscles.
Muscles need rest to adapt and recover after exercise.

slides.title: Measuring Heart Rate
content: Radial Pulse: Found at the wrist joint, below the thumb. Measure beats for 15 seconds, multiply by 4.
Carotid Pulse: Found on the side of the windpipe, just below the jawbone.
Heart Rate Monitors: Use EKG technology via chest straps to transmit heart rate to a wrist receiver.
Mobile phone apps can also be used to measure heart rate.

slides.title: 2.2 Hypokinetic Diseases and Exercise
content: Hypokinetic diseases (Non-Communicable Diseases) are linked to lack of exercise and unhealthy diets.
Examples: Cardiovascular disease, cancer, type-2 diabetes, chronic respiratory disease.
Regular physical activity reduces the risk of these diseases.
Obesity is a major risk factor, caused by an energy imbalance.

slides.title: Preventing Hypokinetic Diseases
content: Exercise improves blood glucose control and can prevent type-2 diabetes.
Aerobic exercise (e.g., walking, cycling) and resistance training are recommended.
A balanced diet and exercise are essential for a healthy lifestyle.
No single intervention is enough; a comprehensive approach is most effective.

slides.title: 2.3 Principles of Physical Fitness Training
content: Specificity: Training must be specific to the fitness component you want to develop.
Progressive Overload: Gradually increase the workload (frequency, intensity, or time) to improve fitness.
Reversibility: Fitness gains are lost when training stops (detraining).
Individual Differences: Each person responds differently to exercise due to genetics and other factors.

slides.title: 2.4 Cardiovascular Endurance
content: Cardiovascular endurance: The ability of the heart, lungs, and blood vessels to deliver oxygen during prolonged activity.
Aerobic activities: Walking, jogging, running, cycling, swimming.
Improves heart and lung health, stroke volume, and lowers resting heart rate.
The FITT Principle: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

slides.title: The FITT Principle
content: Frequency: Exercise 3-5 times per week.
Intensity: Exercise at 50-85% of your maximum heart rate (220 - age).
Time: Duration in the target heart rate zone.
Type: Choose activities like walking, jogging, or swimming.
Methods to improve: Skipping rope, aerobics, walking, jogging, running.

slides.section: 2.5 Exercise Which Develops Muscular Endurance and Strength

slides.title: 2.5 Muscular Endurance and Strength
content: Muscular Strength: Maximum force in a single effort.
Muscular Endurance: Ability to apply force continuously.
Concentric Contraction: Muscle shortens under tension.
Eccentric Contraction: Muscle lengthens under tension.

slides.title: Types of Training Programs
content: Isotonic: Full range of motion with concentric and eccentric contractions (e.g., push-ups).
Isometric: Muscle tension increases without length change (e.g., wall press).
Isokinetic: Constant speed against variable resistance (requires specialized equipment).
Strength Training: Low repetitions, high resistance.
Endurance Training: High repetitions, low resistance.

slides.title: 2.6 Flexibility
content: Flexibility: The ability of a joint to move through its full range of motion.
Dynamic Stretching: Moving joints through a range of motion to prepare for activity.
Static Stretching: Holding a single position for a period of time.
Benefits: Improves performance, reduces injury risk, and is specific to each joint.

slides.title: Flexibility Exercises
content: Dynamic Stretches: Walking high knees, straight leg kicks.
Static Stretches: Walking lunge, side lunge, side bends, triceps stretch, quadriceps stretch, lumbar extensor stretch.
Static stretches should be held for a minimum of 10 seconds and repeated.

slides.title: 3.1 History of Athletics
content: Ethiopia has a rich tradition of producing world-class distance runners.
Abebe Bikila: Gold medalist in the marathon (1960, 1964), first black African man to win Olympic gold.
Haile Gebresilassie and Kenenisa Bekele: Dominant forces in global distance running.
Tirunesh Dibaba: Double gold in 5000m and 10,000m at the 2008 Olympics.

slides.title: African Athletics History
content: Confederation of African Athletics (CAA): Established in 1973, with 54 member countries.
Kip Keino: Won 1500m at the 1968 Olympics for Kenya.
Miruts Yifter: Won 5000m and 10,000m at the 1980 Olympics.
Derartu Tulu: First black African woman to win Olympic gold in 1992 (10,000m).

slides.title: 3.2 Sprint and Sprint Relay
content: Sprinting: Short-distance running (up to 400 meters).
Basic sprint phases: Start, Acceleration, Maintaining Momentum, Finish.
The start involves 'On your marks,' 'Set,' and 'Go.'
Relay Races: Team of four runners passing a baton within a 20-meter zone.

slides.title: Baton Exchange Techniques
content: Upward/Upsweep Exchange: Baton carrier pushes the baton upward into the receiver's hand (palm down).
Downward/Down-sweep Exchange: Baton is placed down into the receiver's palm (palm up).
Common events: 4x100m and 4x400m relays.
Disqualification occurs if the baton is dropped or exchanged outside the zone.

slides.title: 4.1 Brief History of Football
content: Origins: Ancient China (Ts'u Chu), Japan (kemari), Greece/Rome (Episkyros/Harpastum).
Modern football began in England in the 19th century.
FA established in 1863; IFAB in 1882.
FIFA founded in 1904; first World Cup held in Uruguay in 1930.

slides.title: African Football History
content: Football introduced to Africa by Europeans in the late 19th century.
CAF founded in 1957 in Khartoum, Sudan.
Founding members: Sudan, Egypt, South Africa, Ethiopia.
First Africa Cup of Nations: 1957, won by Egypt.
Women's Cup of Nations: Established in 1991, won by Nigeria 11 times.

slides.title: Ethiopian Football History
content: Football introduced by foreigners; St. George FC formed in 1935.
EFF founded in 1943; affiliated with FIFA in 1953 and CAF in 1957.
Ethiopia won the Africa Cup of Nations in 1962.
Ethiopia hosts and wins CECAFA Cup (1987, 2001, 2004, 2005).
Competitions: Premier League, Higher League, First League, Women's Premier League.

slides.title: 4.2 Rules of Football
content: Playing area: Rectangular, green surface, dimensions vary by age group.
Players: 11 per team (including goalkeeper), maximum 5 substitutes, minimum 7 players to start.
Referee: Main referee, two assistant referees, and other officials.
Duration: 2 halves of 45 minutes, 15-minute halftime break.
Ball in/out: Ball is out when it wholly crosses the goal or touchline.

slides.title: More Football Rules
content: Scoring: Goal when ball wholly passes over the goal line.
Offside: Player is offside if nearer to opponent's goal line than the ball and second-last opponent.
Throw-in: Awarded when ball crosses the touchline.
Corner Kick: Awarded when ball crosses the goal line, last touched by a defender.

slides.title: 4.3 Skills of Football: Chest Control
content: Chest control: Used to receive and control an airborne ball.
Position body behind the ball, knees slightly bent.
Lean back slightly to absorb the pace of the ball.
Withdraw the chest immediately upon touch.
Cushion the ball with a slightly concave back.
Touch the ball down to the feet and move.

slides.title: Heading Skills
content: Heading is used for scoring, clearing, and winning possession.
Side/Glancing Heading: Changes direction, often for passing or shooting.
Front/Standard Heading: Provides power and accuracy using the forehead.
Key steps: Keep eyes on the ball, drive through, attack with the body.
Mini-game: Head tennis or heading drills for practice.

slides.title: 5.1 A Brief History of Volleyball
content: Invented in 1895 in the USA by William G. Morgan.
Original name: 'Mintonette'. Renamed 'Volleyball' in 1896.
FIVB founded in 1947; Olympic sport in 1964.
Introduced to Africa by Egypt in 1915; CAVB established in 1972.
Introduced to Ethiopia in 1943; EVF established in 1954; FIVB member in 1964.

slides.title: 5.2 Rules of Volleyball
content: Playing area: 18m x 9m court, surrounded by a 3m free zone.
Net height: 2.43m (men), 2.24m (women).
Ball: Circumference 65-67 cm, weight 260-280 g.
Team: Up to 12 players, 6 on court at a time.
Match: Best of five sets, each set to 25 points (15 for 5th), two-point lead required.
Rotation: Clockwise after winning the serve.

slides.title: 5.3 Spike Skill of Volleyball
content: Spiking: Primary offensive tool to score points.
Four stages: Approach, take-off, body movement in the air, hitting action.
Approach: Three or four-step movement (left-right-left for right-handers).
Key elements: Reach high, contact ball in front of shoulder, apply top-spin.
Types: Standing spike, off-speed spike, hard-driven spike.

slides.title: 6.1 Brief History of Basketball
content: Invented in 1891 in the USA by James Naismith.
Peach baskets and soccer ball used initially.
FIBA formed in 1932; Olympic sport in 1936.
Introduced to Africa in the mid-20th century by missionaries.
AFABA established in 1961 in Cairo, Egypt.
Introduced to Ethiopia in 1946-1947; EBF founded in 1953; FIBA member in 1949.

slides.title: 6.2 Rules of Basketball
content: Court: 28m x 15m.
Game: Four 10-minute quarters; overtime if tied (5 minutes).
Violations: Ball handling (double dribble, traveling) and time (3 seconds).
Fouls: Personal (illegal contact) and technical (unsportsmanlike).
Penalties: Free throws; a player with 5 fouls must leave.

slides.title: 6.3 Skills of Basketball: Lay-up
content: Lay-up: A high-percentage shot taken close to the basket.
For a right-handed layup: Step with the right foot, jump off the left foot, shoot with the right arm.
Aim for the 'sweet spot' on the backboard (above the corner of the small square).
Practice until the movement becomes second nature.
Modified games (2v2, 3v3) can be used to practice lay-ups and other skills.

slides.title: 7.1 A Brief History of Handball
content: Ancient origins: 'Urania' (Greece), 'Harpaston' (Rome).
Developed in Denmark, Sweden, and Germany in the late 19th century.
IHF founded in 1946.
Field handball in 1936 Olympics; indoor handball in 1972; women's in 1976.
CAHB founded in 1973.
Introduced to Ethiopia in 1960; EHF established in 1962; IHF member in 1964.

slides.title: 7.2 The Rules of Handball
content: Court: 40m x 20m, with 6m goal area and 9m free-throw line.
Playing time: Two 30-minute halves.
Ball: Size 3 (men), size 2 (women), size 1 (youth).
Team: Up to 14 players, 7 on court.
Fouls: Pulling, holding, blocking; punishments include warnings, 2-minute suspensions, and disqualifications.

slides.title: 7.3 Basic Skills of Handball
content: Goalkeeping: Key role to block shots and prevent goals.
Qualities: Quickness and courage.
Posture: Feet apart, knees bent, arms at chest level.
Footwork: Small, even steps to move side-to-side and reduce angles.
Drills: Three in a row, positional shooting, one-to-one with a shooter.

slides.title: 7.4 Modified Game Related to Handball
content: Modified games simulate game-like conditions for practice.
2 vs 1: Practice passing and interception.
4 vs 4, 5 vs 5, 7 vs 7: Practice passing, catching, and dribbling in offensive and defensive positions.
These games help develop teamwork and skill application.

slides.title: 8.1 Essence and Roles of Self-Defense
content: Self-defense: The act of protecting oneself from physical harm.
Benefits: Improved physical and mental strength, self-discipline, confidence, and balance.
Ethics: Humility, respect, integrity, courage, self-control.
Safety guidelines: Work gradually, wear comfortable clothing, be aware of surroundings, avoid dark places alone.

slides.title: 8.2 Principles and Rules of Self-Defense
content: Principles: Alertness, Decisiveness, Aggressiveness, Coolness, Speed, Surprise.
Rules: Know your route, walk confidently, trust your instincts, avoid predictable routines.
Carry items that make noise (whistle, phone).
Know vulnerable areas of an attacker: eyes, ears, throat, groin, knees, shins.

slides.title: 8.3 Basic Techniques of Self-Defense
content: Basic Stance: A defensive position that prepares for an attack.
Escapes: Bear hug, hands trapped, side headlock.
Strikes: Front kick to groin, heel palm strike, elbow strike.
Grappling: Close-quarters fighting using holds and locks.
Practice with a partner, following safety measures.
